author: "Michael Barkasi"

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
options(width = 10000)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(class.output = "scroll-output", cache = TRUE, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(flipFISH)
```

## Why this document exists

`sim.benchmark()` is supposed to answer a simple question: if we simulate data from known bit-flip
rates and bit-flip correlations, how well does `misread.qc()` recover them? Running it turned up a
real, reproducible problem -- barcodes with a genuinely low true positive predictive value (PPV)
were consistently coming back estimated well above 0.5 -- and chasing that problem down ended up
teaching us a lot more about this model than we expected: how much `max_flips` actually matters,
how much of the correlation structure the data can even see, and how much of the remaining gap is
a search problem versus a data problem.

Along the way we also tried an alternative simulated-annealing optimizer (MCMCSA) as a possible
fix. It didn't pan out and has since been removed from the package; it isn't covered here.

This document walks through the findings in roughly the order we found them, with the actual code
used to produce each result. Several of these computations take a long time (the cross-mouse
comparison near the end took about 4.5 hours), so every expensive chunk below is wrapped in a
small caching helper: it loads a saved result if one exists, and only recomputes (and re-saves)
if it doesn't. The real code is always there -- delete the cache and it will genuinely re-run --
but you won't have to wait hours to re-knit this file.

```{r helpers}
# Cache location: prefer the source tree (so regenerated results land in version control),
# fall back to the installed package's copy otherwise.
cache_dir <- normalizePath(file.path("..", "inst", "extdata", "vignette_cache"), mustWork = FALSE)
if (!dir.exists(cache_dir)) {
  cache_dir <- system.file("extdata", "vignette_cache", package = "flipFISH")
}

run_cached <- function(name, expr) {
  path <- file.path(cache_dir, paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
  result <- expr
  dir.create(dirname(path), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(result, path)
  result
}

# Summary metrics used throughout: how well were bit-flip correlations recovered, and how biased
# is the estimated PPV for barcodes whose true PPV is low but nonzero?
build_metrics <- function(bm) {
  n_total <- length(bm$fr_stip)
  N_bits  <- as.integer((-1 + sqrt(1 + 4 * n_total)) / 2) # solves N*(N+1) = n_total
  n_sims  <- nrow(bm$ecc_est)
  cor_stip <- rep(bm$fr_stip[(2 * N_bits + 1):n_total], each = n_sims)
  cor_est  <- c(bm$fr__est[, (2 * N_bits + 1):n_total])
  cor_stip[is.na(cor_stip)] <- 0
  cor_est[is.na(cor_est)]   <- 0
  PPV_exp <- bm$PPV_exp
  PPV_est <- colMeans(bm$PPV_est, na.rm = TRUE)
  df_low <- subset(data.frame(PPV_exp = PPV_exp, PPV_est = PPV_est), PPV_exp > 0 & PPV_exp < 0.4)
  list(
    cor_recovery      = cor(cor_stip, cor_est),
    overall_ppv_cor   = cor(PPV_exp, PPV_est, use = "complete.obs"),
    mean_low_ppv_true = mean(df_low$PPV_exp, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_low_ppv_est  = mean(df_low$PPV_est, na.rm = TRUE),
    low_bias          = mean(df_low$PPV_est, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(df_low$PPV_exp, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_low_ppv_band    = nrow(df_low)
  )
}
```

## Setup: one codebook, one mouse, one imaging-protocol layout

Everything below uses the same 28-bit codebook and the same real summary statistics (mouse 1,
unless noted) that come bundled with the package, plus a small table of which imaging round and
color channel each bit belongs to -- the physical layout a MERSCOPE-style experiment actually
has, which becomes important a few sections in.

```{r load_data}
codebook <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "codebook_obs.csv", package = "flipFISH"), row.names = 1)
ss       <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "summary_stats_all_mice.csv", package = "flipFISH"), row.names = 1)
rownames(codebook) <- gsub("-", ".", rownames(codebook))
m1 <- ss[ss$mouse == 1, ]

bit_org <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "bit_organization.csv", package = "flipFISH"))
bit_org <- bit_org[order(bit_org$bitNumber), ]
N_bits  <- nrow(bit_org)

# species/codebook reordering sim.benchmark() applies internally (genes then blanks, each sorted by
# decreasing rate) -- reproduced here so we can rebuild its internal bc_counts matrix for the
# single-evaluation diagnostics in the next couple of sections.
species_names <- rownames(m1)
cb_aligned    <- codebook[species_names, ]
blank_mask    <- grepl("Blank", species_names)
gene_order    <- order(m1$rates[!blank_mask], decreasing = TRUE)
blank_order   <- order(m1$rates[blank_mask],  decreasing = TRUE)
m1_sorted     <- rbind(m1[!blank_mask, ][gene_order, ], m1[blank_mask, ][blank_order, ])
cb_sorted     <- rbind(cb_aligned[!blank_mask, ][gene_order, ], cb_aligned[blank_mask, ][blank_order, ])

make_bc_counts <- function(sim_counts, orig) {
  bcc <- orig
  bcc$rates  <- orig$rates * pmax(1, sim_counts) / orig$counts
  bcc$counts <- sim_counts
  as.matrix(bcc[, c("rates", "variance", "counts")])
}
```

## 1. `max_flips` doesn't need to be large

`max_flips` caps how many simultaneous bit flips the analytic model bothers to sum over when
computing expected counts. Bigger should be more accurate, but also slower -- the question is
where the extra accuracy actually stops mattering.

We check by taking one already-simulated dataset and evaluating the objective, at both the true
and a fitted parameter vector, across a few `max_flips` values. (`baseline` here is the
unstructured-truth/uniform-prior benchmark run used again in the next section -- cached the first
time, reused after that.)

```{r maxflips_sweep}
baseline <- run_cached("baseline", sim.benchmark(
  m1, codebook,
  n_sims = 2, n_forks = 8, max_flips = 6, report_freq = 10, maxeval = 150,
  maxHam = NULL, blank_weight = 10, prior_weight = 0.5, dispersion_weight = 0.5,
  erc_weight = 0, n_restarts = 1, use_mcmcsa = FALSE
))

bcc_1 <- make_bc_counts(baseline$occ_sim[1, ], m1_sorted)

maxflips_sweep <- run_cached("maxflips_sweep", {
  mf_vals <- c(4L, 6L, 8L, 10L)
  sweep <- data.frame(max_flips = mf_vals, msle_stip = NA_real_, msle_est = NA_real_, eval_seconds = NA_real_)
  for (k in seq_along(mf_vals)) {
    t0 <- Sys.time()
    sweep$msle_stip[k] <- mQC_msle_at(baseline$fr_stip, bcc_1, as.matrix(cb_sorted), 3L, 8L, mf_vals[k],
                                       list(), 10, 0.5, 0.5, numeric(), 0)
    sweep$msle_est[k]  <- mQC_msle_at(baseline$fr__est[1, ], bcc_1, as.matrix(cb_sorted), 3L, 8L, mf_vals[k],
                                       list(), 10, 0.5, 0.5, numeric(), 0)
    sweep$eval_seconds[k] <- as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "secs")
  }
  sweep
})
knitr::kable(maxflips_sweep, digits = 4)
```

Both scores are already flat by `max_flips = 8` -- `max_flips = 10` changes nothing in the fourth
decimal place, while the time cost keeps climbing steeply. There's no accuracy left to buy past
about 6-8; anything beyond that is just burning CPU.

## 2. The real ceiling: what the data can't tell you

Before blaming the optimizer for a bad fit, it's worth checking whether the data even contains the
answer. We can do this directly: compute the analytic Jacobian (sensitivity of each barcode's
expected count to each parameter) at the true parameters, and look at its singular value
spectrum. A parameter direction the data can't see shows up as a near-zero singular value,
regardless of what any optimizer does.

```{r jacobian_svd}
jacobians <- run_cached("jacobians_true_fit", list(
  J_true = mQC_ecc_jacobian_at(baseline$fr_stip,    bcc_1, as.matrix(cb_sorted), 3L, 8L, 6L),
  J_fit  = mQC_ecc_jacobian_at(baseline$fr__est[1, ], bcc_1, as.matrix(cb_sorted), 3L, 8L, 6L)
))

corr_free <- N_bits * (N_bits - 1) / 2
rate_cols <- 1:(2 * N_bits)
corr_cols <- (2 * N_bits + 1):(2 * N_bits + 2 * corr_free)

svd_summary <- function(J, cols, thresh = 1e-3) {
  s <- svd(J[, cols, drop = FALSE], nu = 0, nv = 0)$d
  data.frame(
    n_params       = length(cols),
    condition_no    = s[1] / s[length(s)],
    effective_rank = sum(s / s[1] > thresh)
  )
}

rbind(
  data.frame(block = "flip rates (56 params)",       svd_summary(jacobians$J_true, rate_cols)),
  data.frame(block = "bit-flip correlations (756)",   svd_summary(jacobians$J_true, corr_cols))
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 1)
```

The flip-rate block is textbook well-posed: a condition number in the tens, full rank. The
correlation block, evaluated at the *true* parameters -- the single most favorable point this
comparison could be made at -- has a condition number in the billions, and only a few hundred of
its 756 directions carry signal above the noise floor. Here's the spectrum itself:

```{r svd_spectrum_plot}
s_corr <- svd(jacobians$J_true[, corr_cols, drop = FALSE], nu = 0, nv = 0)$d
spectrum_df <- data.frame(rank = seq_along(s_corr), rel_sv = s_corr / s_corr[1])

ggplot2::ggplot(spectrum_df, ggplot2::aes(x = rank, y = rel_sv)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Bit-flip correlation block: singular value spectrum",
    x     = "singular value rank",
    y     = "relative singular value (log scale)"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.background  = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)
  )
```

That's a structural property of this codebook and count data, not of any fitting algorithm --
most of the correlation parameter space genuinely isn't constrained by what gets observed.

## 3. A smarter search can't fix a ceiling that's already reached

If the fitted solution already scores as well as (or better than) the true parameters under the
identical objective, then a better search algorithm has nothing to find -- the shortfall is in the
objective/data, not the optimizer.

```{r search_vs_truth}
data.frame(
  sim       = 1:2,
  msle_est  = baseline$msle_est,
  msle_stip = baseline$msle_stip
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 4, caption = "Plain L-BFGS (150 evals) vs. the truth's own score")
```

The fitted score is already in the same ballpark as the truth's own score (sometimes slightly
better). Whatever's left to explain about the correlation-recovery problem, it isn't "the search
didn't try hard enough" at this stage -- that question gets more interesting once we give the
search more room, in a couple of sections.

## 4. A structured prior helps -- but only once it's given room to work

The codebook's bits aren't drawn from nowhere; they're organized into imaging rounds (3 bits
imaged together per round) and color channels. That's exactly the kind of thing `build_corr_priors()`
and `build_structured_truth_priors()` were built to express -- a prior (for fitting) and a
matching generative structure (for simulating a *realistic*, non-arbitrary truth) organized the
same way.

```{r structured_priors}
structured_truth <- build_structured_truth_priors(
  N_bits = N_bits, bit_round = bit_org$imagingRound, bit_channel = bit_org$color,
  round_corr_sd = 0.2, channel_rho = 0.5, w_round = 0.7, w_channel = 0.1
)
tiered_prior <- build_corr_priors(
  N_bits = N_bits, bit_round = bit_org$imagingRound, bit_channel = bit_org$color,
  sd_round = 0.2, sd_channel = 0.1, sd_other = 0.01
)
```

The natural question is whether fitting with a prior that matches this structure actually helps
recover it. The first time we checked, at a modest search budget, the answer looked like "no" --
the structured prior and a plain uniform prior performed about the same. Running the same
comparison with a deeper search budget told a different story:

```{r structured_vs_uniform}
common_shallow <- list(STdata = m1, codebook = codebook, n_sims = 2, n_forks = 8, max_flips = 6,
                        report_freq = 10, maxeval = 150, maxHam = NULL, blank_weight = 10,
                        prior_weight = 0.5, dispersion_weight = 0.5, erc_weight = 0,
                        n_restarts = 1, use_mcmcsa = FALSE)
common_deep <- modifyList(common_shallow, list(maxeval = 350, n_restarts = 3, report_freq = 25))

bm_tiered_shallow  <- run_cached("structured_tiered_shallow",
  do.call(sim.benchmark, modifyList(common_shallow, list(stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = tiered_prior))))
bm_uniform_shallow <- run_cached("structured_uniform_shallow",
  do.call(sim.benchmark, modifyList(common_shallow, list(stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = list()))))
bm_tiered_deep     <- run_cached("structured_tiered_deep",
  do.call(sim.benchmark, modifyList(common_deep, list(stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = tiered_prior))))
bm_uniform_deep    <- run_cached("structured_uniform_deep",
  do.call(sim.benchmark, modifyList(common_deep, list(stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = list()))))

rbind(
  data.frame(prior = "tiered",  search = "shallow (1x150)", as.data.frame(build_metrics(bm_tiered_shallow))[c("cor_recovery","low_bias")]),
  data.frame(prior = "uniform", search = "shallow (1x150)", as.data.frame(build_metrics(bm_uniform_shallow))[c("cor_recovery","low_bias")]),
  data.frame(prior = "tiered",  search = "deep (3x350)",    as.data.frame(build_metrics(bm_tiered_deep))[c("cor_recovery","low_bias")]),
  data.frame(prior = "uniform", search = "deep (3x350)",    as.data.frame(build_metrics(bm_uniform_deep))[c("cor_recovery","low_bias")])
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

At shallow search the two priors are nearly indistinguishable. At depth, the tiered prior pulls
clearly ahead on correlation recovery. The prior's benefit was real all along -- it just wasn't
visible until the optimizer had enough budget to exploit the simpler landscape it creates.

## 5. Nobody in this investigation actually converged

Every single optimization run in this whole investigation stopped because it hit its evaluation
cap, not because it satisfied L-BFGS's own convergence criteria. That matters: it means every
number above is a floor, not a final answer.

```{r convergence_demo}
convergence_demo <- run_cached("convergence_demo", {
  con <- textConnection("captured_log", "w")
  sink(con)
  bm_traj <- sim.benchmark(
    m1, codebook, n_sims = 1, n_forks = 8, max_flips = 6, report_freq = 10, maxeval = 100,
    maxHam = NULL, blank_weight = 10, prior_weight = 0.5, dispersion_weight = 0.5, erc_weight = 0,
    n_restarts = 1, use_mcmcsa = FALSE,
    stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = tiered_prior
  )
  sink(); close(con)
  # Stop parsing at the optimizer's own finish line -- the separate msle_stip evaluation
  # (true parameters' score) gets logged right after in the identical "eval N, msle: Y" format,
  # with its own counter restarting at 1, and would otherwise get swept in as a spurious extra
  # trajectory point.
  stop_idx    <- grep("result code", captured_log)[1]
  pre_stop    <- captured_log[seq_len(stop_idx)]
  eval_lines  <- grep("^\\s*eval [0-9]+, msle: ", pre_stop, value = TRUE)
  mm  <- regmatches(eval_lines, regexec("eval ([0-9]+), msle: ([0-9.eE+-]+)", eval_lines))
  traj <- do.call(rbind, lapply(mm, function(x) data.frame(eval = as.integer(x[2]), msle = as.numeric(x[3]))))
  list(trajectory = traj, stop_line = captured_log[stop_idx], bm = bm_traj)
})

ggplot2::ggplot(convergence_demo$trajectory, ggplot2::aes(x = eval, y = msle)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Still descending when the eval cap hit",
    x     = "eval",
    y     = "msle"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.background  = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA)
  )
cat(trimws(convergence_demo$stop_line), "\n")
```

`result code 5` is nlopt's `MAXEVAL_REACHED` -- not a convergence code. And the trajectory is
still dropping, sometimes steeply, right up to the cutoff. Giving it more room keeps paying off:

```{r evals_matter}
mouse1_500 <- run_cached("mouse1_500", sim.benchmark(
  m1, codebook, n_sims = 1, n_forks = 8, max_flips = 6, report_freq = 25, maxeval = 500,
  maxHam = NULL, blank_weight = 10, prior_weight = 0.5, dispersion_weight = 0.5, erc_weight = 0,
  n_restarts = 1, use_mcmcsa = FALSE,
  stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = tiered_prior
))

data.frame(
  evals        = c(150, 500),
  cor_recovery = c(build_metrics(bm_tiered_shallow)$cor_recovery, build_metrics(mouse1_500)$cor_recovery)
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Same 1-restart lineage, mouse 1: more budget keeps helping")
```

## 6. One long run beat three shorter ones

Section 4's "deep" search spread its budget across 3 restarts of 350 evals each (1050 evals
total). The single-restart, 500-eval run from the last section used *less* total budget and still
came out ahead on correlation recovery:

```{r depth_vs_restarts}
data.frame(
  strategy      = c("3 restarts x 350 evals (1050 total)", "1 restart x 500 evals (500 total)"),
  cor_recovery  = c(build_metrics(bm_tiered_deep)$cor_recovery, build_metrics(mouse1_500)$cor_recovery)
) |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

For this problem, at least so far, depth on one trajectory has outpaced restart diversity. That's
consistent with the previous section: nothing has converged yet, so a longer single run still has
room to keep improving, while splitting the same budget across several shorter, equally-unconverged
runs doesn't.

## 7. Is this just one mouse's problem? Running it on all five says no

The data bundled with this package covers five mice sharing one codebook. Repeating the
500-eval, structured-truth-plus-tiered-prior setup on each one separately checks whether anything
above is an artifact of mouse 1's particular data.

```{r five_mice}
five_mice <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(mouse_id) {
  bm <- run_cached(paste0("mouse", mouse_id, "_500"), {
    m_i <- ss[ss$mouse == mouse_id, ]
    rownames(m_i) <- rownames(m1) # the combined CSV's row names get auto-mangled for mice 2-5
                                    # (duplicate gene names across mice trigger R's own
                                    # make-unique suffixing at file-creation time); gene order is
                                    # identical across all 5 mice's blocks, so mouse 1's names are
                                    # restored onto the others by position.
    sim.benchmark(
      m_i, codebook, n_sims = 1, n_forks = 8, max_flips = 6, report_freq = 25, maxeval = 500,
      maxHam = NULL, blank_weight = 10, prior_weight = 0.5, dispersion_weight = 0.5, erc_weight = 0,
      n_restarts = 1, use_mcmcsa = FALSE,
      stip_fliprate_priors = structured_truth, fliprate_priors = tiered_prior
    )
  })
  m <- build_metrics(bm)
  data.frame(mouse = mouse_id, cor_recovery = m$cor_recovery, low_bias = m$low_bias,
             true_ppv_band = m$mean_low_ppv_true, est_ppv_band = m$mean_low_ppv_est)
}))

knitr::kable(five_mice, digits = 3)
cat(sprintf("cor_recovery: mean=%.3f sd=%.3f\nlow_bias:     mean=%.3f sd=%.3f\n",
            mean(five_mice$cor_recovery), sd(five_mice$cor_recovery),
            mean(five_mice$low_bias), sd(five_mice$low_bias)))
```

`cor_recovery` varies noticeably from mouse to mouse -- which real dataset you start from matters.
`low_bias` barely moves. The severity of the core problem (barcodes with true PPV around 0.26-0.29
coming back estimated around 0.62-0.64) isn't a mouse-1 artifact; it shows up just as strongly in
every independent replicate tested, and even the best search we tried only dented it.

## Where this leaves things

More `max_flips` than ~8 buys nothing. Much of the bit-flip correlation structure genuinely isn't
identifiable from this data, measured directly and independent of any fitting algorithm. A
structured prior helps, but only once the optimizer is given enough room to use it, and "enough
room" turned out to be more than every run in this investigation actually got -- nothing here ever
converged on its own terms. And the residual bias this all started from is real, reproducible
across five independent mice, and only partially closed even under the best conditions we could
construct. The practical toolkit this produced -- `mQC_msle_at()`, `mQC_ecc_jacobian_at()`,
`build_corr_priors()`, and `build_structured_truth_priors()` -- is what's left to work with going
forward.
